Science.title: Spiders, beetles and one garage alligator: Largest study to date reveals wildlife sharing our indoor spaces
Science.summary: An international team of researchers is revealing the largest study to date detailing the wide range of insects, arachnids and other organisms that live in homes and other indoor environments across the United States and Canada. The researchers have compiled a database with more than 20,000 entries spanning more than 2,000 species found in these indoor ecosystems.

Science.title: ‘Incredibly frustrating’: prestigious fellowship applications close in just 21 hours
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03805-6 The Humboldt Foundation says that applications for its fellowships have increased markedly in the past two years, but they did not anticipate the influx this month.

Science.title: Mapping the microbes' arms race with viruses at planetary scale
Science.summary: Microbiomes are complex ecosystems, in which bacteria and archaea are constantly interacting with, and infected by, viruses. These viruses can significantly impact microbiome processes, not only by killing their host but also sometimes by temporarily providing additional capabilities to their host. As many viruses have not been grown in a lab, connecting them to their natural hosts has been difficult. A new bioinformatics toolkit and database are now available to help researchers make those associations at an unprecedented scale.

Science.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
Science.summary: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

Science.title: 'Forever' chemicals? Don't be so sure, says engineer
Science.summary: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students clad in hard hats peered up at six towering vats of bleach used to treat water that flows from the distant Liberty Reservoir into the facility, killing bacteria and other pathogens before it's routed to the region's kitchen sinks.

Science.title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
Science.summary: Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing the lunar environment may suffer irreversible damage if things move too fast.

Science.title: Brains of people with PTSD have unique epigenetic marks, study finds
Science.summary: The brains of people with PTSD bear molecular changes that differ from those in people with other conditions, like depression, a new study finds.

Science.title: Digital imaging workshop aims to reveal secrets in medieval manuscripts
Science.summary: Researchers recently used multispectral imaging technology to try to uncover hidden information from medieval manuscripts at the Rare Book and Manuscript Library at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The library hosted a digital imaging workshop in early October that served as a pilot study for how the technology can help analyze fragile, centuries-old documents.

Science.title: New hemp plant produces no detectable THC, potentially reducing risk of crop destruction
Science.summary: Scientists at Texas A M AgriLife Research, a member of The Texas A M University System, have developed a hemp plant that produces no detectable cannabinoids, including THC.

Science.title: Can Instagram reduce prejudice? Study reveals the potential and limits of social media contact
Science.summary: A research team at the University of Potsdam has conducted a field experiment to investigate whether contact through social media can reduce prejudice. The findings suggest that following an unfamiliar Instagram profile for just three days can lead to more favorable attitudes—not only toward the group represented by the profile. The study was published in the Journal of the Association for Information Systems.

Science.title: New sources of neurotoxin linked to algal blooms uncovered in Florida and Kansas
Science.summary: Researchers have identified two previously unreported strains of freshwater cyanobacteria capable of producing a potent neurotoxin that poses risks to people, pets, wildlife and water resources and that some scientists suspect may have contributed to previous animal deaths.

Science.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
Science.summary: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.

Science.title: A new way to extract oxygen from lunar soil could support bases on the moon
Science.summary: Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.

Science.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
Science.summary: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

Science.title: Witnessing generosity from low-income donors more likely to elicit giving from observers, research finds
Science.summary: Billionaire Warren Buffett announced this month he will donate $5.47 billion to four foundations associated with his family ahead of Thanksgiving. Similarly, various students in club organizations throughout Kansas are collecting food items to give to hungry families for the holiday.

Science.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
Science.summary: An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity, and that verifies Einstein's greatest theory.

Science.title: Ruminations on a last movement
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03519-9 Keeping a note.

Science.title: El Niño created a skiers' paradise in Chile—now it's Sierra Nevada and southern Rockies' turn
Science.summary: El Niño has a reputation for being a skier's dream, bringing lots of snow to California's Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season. But El Niño's supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.

Science.title: New study rewrites the role of a major speech hub in the brain
Science.summary: Wernicke's area was thought to be mostly linked to understanding speech. A landmark new study has something more to say.

Science.title: Ghostly 'sand body' double burial unearthed at Sutton Hoo
Science.summary: During a month-long excavation with the documentary series "Time Team," archaeologists unearthed another mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo.

Science.title: The view from the tower: Watch Starship come in for chopsticks catch in epic slo-mo video
Science.summary: A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a tower's-eye view of the first-ever catch of a Starship upper stage, a milestone SpaceX achieved last weekend.

Science.title: Lifting weights reduces muscle loss from obesity drugs
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03751-3 Resistance exercise could help middle-aged and older individuals to maintain muscle mass and strength during weight-loss treatment.

Science.title: Ancient bison hunting site in Texas challenges long-held assumptions
Science.summary: For decades, archaeologists questioned whether Native American communities in the Southern Plains hunted bison by driving herds over cliffs, a sophisticated technique widely documented farther north.

Science.title: Gamified mobile payment features may drive adoption among Gen-Z users
Science.summary: Gamified features in mobile payment applications may significantly increase adoption among consumers in emerging economies, with men and women responding in almost identical ways, according to research published in the International Journal of Business Information Systems.

Science.title: The immune system 'remembers' germs by tweaking its epigenetics, study shows
Science.summary: A new study helps explain how the immune system's first line of defense stays ready to fight off germs and diseases.

Science.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
Science.summary: Aldebaran looks for all the world like the brightest member of the Hyades star cluster. It isn't — and discovering why changes the way you look at constellations.

Science.title: Is it genuine love—or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
Science.summary: Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation—these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don't want to let that person out of your sight.

Science.title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
Science.summary: A biblical mystery, an ancient Egyptian inscription and a "ring of fire" solar eclipse 3,200 years ago hold clues to when Ramesses the Great ruled.

Science.title: How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03465-6 A nagging sense that you don’t belong can keep you grounded and might help to improve your performance.
